hornswoggle.e: Unknown, 1829 US, jocular coinage like contemporary absquatulate. Presumably horns + waggle with humorous faux ablaut or combination with wobble (compare later woggle, 1923), perhaps inspired by lassoed steers trying to escape by moving their head.

d.g: To cause to feel extreme apprehension or unease; to cause to experience horror.
d.x: The haunted house horrified me, as I passed from one room to the next feeling more and more like I wasn’t going to survive.

horrify.e: From horror + -ify, or borrowed from Latin horrificare (cf. French horrifier). 1791, in form horrifying.

d.g: To bristle in fear or horror; to have goose bumps or goose pimples.
d.x: When Hel shrugged and changed the subject diplomatically, the nape of Diamond's neck horripilated with embarrassment.

horripilate.e: From Late Latin horripilātus, perfect passive participle of horripilō (“(of hairs) to bristle”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from horreō (“to bristle, shiver, dread”) + pilus (“hair”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰers- (“to bristle”).

hospitalise.e: Proto-Italic *hostipotjālis Late Latin hospitālisbor. Old French hospitalbor. Middle English hospital English hospital English -ise English hospitalise From hospital + -ise.

hospitalize.e: From hospital + -ize. Piecewise doublet of hotelize.
